blocks.title: Free vibrations
blocks.text: A body is said to be executing free vibrations if it oscillates with its natural frequency without the interference of an external force.
For example, a simple pendulum shown in Fig. 14.12 vibrates freely with its natural frequency that depends only upon its length when it is slightly displaced from its mean position.

blocks.alt: A simple pendulum hangs from O on a support. The bob is drawn at A, at the mean position B and at C, with a dotted arc between A and C and arrows showing it swinging both ways through B.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.12: Illustration of free oscillation of simple pendulum (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.12).

blocks.text: In free oscillations, the total energy of the body remains constant i.e., energy is conserved. As we are assuming in the absence of resistance force the amplitude of the oscillation remains constant.

If a freely oscillating system is subjected to an external force, then forced vibrations will take place. Such as when swing is struck repeatedly, then forced vibrations are produced as shown in Fig. 14.13.

blocks.alt: Two moments at a playground swing. In each a man stands behind a swing and pushes a girl sitting on it; in the second the swing has moved forward and he is still pushing with outstretched arms.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.13: Illustration of forced oscillations of a swing (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.13).

blocks.text: The vibrations of a factory floor caused by the running of heavy machinery are an example of forced vibrations. Another example of forced vibration is loud music produced by sounding wooden boards of string instruments.

blocks.title: Interesting Information
blocks.text:
• Guitar string
• Bell ringing
• Atomic oscillation
• Bridge vibration
• Building sway are the examples of free oscillations
